this regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
speechtext: Section 5 of the Bank of Canada Act provides that the Bank shall be under the management of its Board of Directors. Section 8(1) of the Act states that the Governor of the Bank is the chief executive officer of the Bank and on behalf of the Board has the direction and control of the business of the Bank with authority to act in connection with the conduct of the business of the Bank in all matters that are not by this Act or by the by-laws of the Bank specifically reserved to be done by the Board or by the Executive Committee. Section 14 of the Act requires that the Minister and the Governor shall consult regularly on monetary policy and on its relation to general economic policy. It also provides, in the event of a difference of opinion between the Minister and the Bank concerning the monetary policy to be followed, that the Min-iser may, after consultation with the Governor and with the approval of the Governor in Council, give to the Governor a written directive concerning monetary policy which shall be published forthwith and that the Bank shall comply with such directive.

1.	A five year period of residential qualification was first introduced in Canada by the "British Nationality and Status of Aliens Act, 1914" which was re-enacted mutatis mutandis in this country. It is said to have been enacted to guard against the cases of persons becoming naturalized in a country requiring little or no previous residence, and then returning to their own country, or settling in some foreign country, with a claim to nationality and protection to which they had not become entitled according to recognized principles of international law by a bona fide change of domicile.
2.	All the provisions of the Canadian Citizenship Act are now the subject of review which has not yet been completed. It is not possible therefore to say what changes are intended.
3.	See 2 above.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 NATIONAL DEFENCE FIRING OF A.B.M. WARHEADS OVER CANADIAN TERRITORY-MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask for leave,
seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to move the adjournment of the house under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring, urgent consideration, namely the urgent situation revealed by the United States defence department that the United States is now seeking Canadian approval to fire anti-ballistic missiles with large thermonuclear warheads over Canadian territory. It is quite clear from the Prime Minister's statements in the house on Monday and statements by Canadian embassy officials in Washington that the United States in deciding to construct this new A.B.M. system did not seek or obtain the Canadian government's permission for such thermonuclear missile flights over Canada, which means that interception would take place over Canadian territory causing extensive nuclear fallout.
Given this fact, plus the broader world danger implications that the construction of this A.B.M. system will further escalate the nuclear arms race, and given the fact that the Prime Minister will be meeting the President of the United States on Monday and Tuesday of this coming week, it is extremely important and vitally urgent that there be a full and comprehensive discussion in the House of Commons prior to this visit in order to evaluate Canada's position in this matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 NATIONAL DEFENCE FIRING OF A.B.M. WARHEADS OVER CANADIAN TERRITORY-MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
In determining whether a matter should have urgent consideration
March 19. 1969

under Standing Order 26, the Speaker is required to have regard to a number of factors. These are specified in sections 5 and 16 of the relevant rule. In particular the matter proposed for discussion must be one which calls for immediate and urgent consideration. The Chair must also have regard to the probability of the matter being brought before the house within reasonable time by other means.
In this instance the proposal is that the house be given an opportunity to debate a question of undoubted national interest on an urgent basis because the right hon. Prime Minister will be engaged in discussions with the President of the United States on Monday next. The business announced for the rest of the week would not provide an opportunity for such a debate.
It seems to me on reflection that this might well be the type of situation where the standing order should operate, so as to permit debate on a national issue in advance of anticipated events. I am therefore prepared to put the motion to the house: Has the hon. member leave to move a motion for the purpose of discussing the matter stated by the hon. member?

Some people feel that research is too expensive for a country such as Canada. 1 say to such people that drug research has risen from zero to the point where approximately $12 million per year is now being spent. We had a report early in 1966 prepared by Wood, Gundy and Company Limited and endorsed by over 100 of our most prominent medical researchers, deans of medical colleges and heads of various departments of medical colleges all across the country. All these people have stressed the very serious short-fall in the amount of money and effort we have put into medical research.
Let me read just a couple of sentences from the Wood, Gundy report. The minister can find this passage on page 3. It reads as follows:
Although financial support has been increasing, medical research in Canada today is being conducted on an inadequate scale. As the Royal Commission on Health Services commented: "available funds lag behind the amounts needed for the support of research."
We were moving in the right direction until this year. We have been increasing in recent years the amount of money made available to the Medical Research Council for distribution to various medical research projects across the country. We have been increasing the amount by 30 per cent a year. That was a very substantial increase. However, it was not as good as it sounds because, while the amount of money given to the Medical Research Council was increased by 30 per cent a year, other research funds which had been available through the Defence Research Board and the Department of National Health and Welfare were reduced.
I have been told by people expert in the field of medical research that had the increase of 30 per cent a year been continued it is likely that in the next three or four years we would have been approaching the amount that is required in this country. But what do
March 19, 1969

Government Organization we find this year? We find that instead of the 30 per cent increase we have had in recent years the increase has been reduced to 14 per cent. Last year the Medical Research Council received $27 million; this year it is to receive only $31 million.
The decision to reduce the amount of increase was not made because the scientific community, the people conversant with the needs of medical research, reported to the government that they were attaining the position which ought to be attained, one where people carrying out useful medical research were having their needs met; it was made for narrow, purely budgetary reasons because of the government's decision to try to hold the line. This means that research funds which have been available in large amounts from the United States for medical research in almost every medical college in Canada are being reduced to the point where in the very near future they will be almost non-existent. The government of Canada is cutting back very drastically on the increases which obviously it had come to the conclusion would have to be made at the same time.
I was told only this morning by one of the top medical researchers at McGill University that this year the Medical Research Council is approving only about 55 per cent of the applications it is receiving for research grants. I do not say that 45 per cent of the applications are being rejected completely, but where applications are not being rejected the amounts requested are being cut very seriously. This is a disaster and an invitation to qualified people, trained in this country at great expense, to leave Canada and go to the United States where medical research has between 400 per cent and 500 per cent more money available to it than it has in Canada.
I can and will put on the record today some of the conclusions of the Wood, Gundy report which I mentioned earlier. But first I want to give the minister three examples of what this cut-back in the projected funds for research means. I received this information this morning through three telephone calls. I am sure that if I had stayed on the telephone for another couple of hours and called medical colleges across the country I could have cited not three but 30 or 300 similar examples. Let me put on the record some of the things I was told this morning.
I refer to the Department of Pharmacology at McGill University, and Professor Lowen-thal, one of the top experts in anti-coagulants. [Mr. Orlikow.l
The hon. member for Simcoe North can correct me if I am wrong, but X was told last week that about 50 per cent of the people who die do so as a result of heart or blood vessel failure. The use of anti-coagulant drugs is extremely important in saving the lives of people. Professor Lowenthal was persuaded to move from Queen's University to McGill where he is a full professor in biochemistry.
At Queen's University he was receiving grants from the Medical Research Council and the Ontario Heart Foundation. At McGill, where I am sure Professor Lowenthal expected to have at least the amount of money with which to carry out his research that he had received at Queen's University, he finds that while he is still getting the money which he received at Queen's University from the Medical Research Council, the 50 per cent of his research fund which he formerly received from the Ontario Heart Foundation is not available. As a result of the shortage of funds Professor Lowenthal, one of the top people in his field in the country, will be working next year with one arm tied behind his back, thanks to the niggardly policy of the federal government.
I spoke this morning to Dr. Selye at the University of Montreal, a world famous medical researcher. Dr. Selye tells me that of the $800,000 which his department expends only $80,000 comes from the Medical Research Council. Dr. Selye told me about a case which would be ludicrous if it were not so tragic.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
At the time of the Russian invasion of Czechoslovakia the government of Canada, with the approval of, I would say, 95 per cent of the people of Canada, agreed to encourage as many Czech refugees as possible to come to Canada. Some of them were doctors and some medical researchers. The Medical Research Council made funds available for some of these medical scientists to do work in Canada. Four of them are working with Dr. Selye at the University of Montreal. The funds with which they are working will be expended in June of this year and the Medical Research Council has told Dr. Selye that they are very sorry but no money will be available for them next year. I do not know what the Minister of National Health and Welfare suggests that these four people should do. Perhaps they should go to the United States where their scientific knowledge and technical abilities will obviously be much more
March 19, 1969

appreciated than they are in Canada. What was the good of bringing them here if we cannot find the funds to let them do the work which they are qualified to do, work which will contribute to the better health and wellbeing of the people of Canada?
The Department of Psychiatry at the University of Manitoba has a highly qualified psychiatrist who would like to spend his time doing clinical research in the field of mental health. No money is available for that purpose from the Medical Research Council. So one of two things is going to happen: Either that highly trained, highly skilful psychiatrist is not going to do what he wants but is going to stay in Winnipeg at the University of Manitoba teaching part time and, I suppose, practising part time, or he is going to go somewhere where he can do research work which will help the people of the world understand better what causes mental illness and what can be done to help the 10 per cent of our population who are likely to be mentally or emotionally fill. We are inviting him to go to the United States where funds and facilities will be available for him to do the work which he would like to do. I suggest to the minister that what he is doing is certainly a disservice to the people of Canada, if not a disaster.
At the same time that the minister and the government are cutting back on the amount of money available to the Medical Research Council, the minister has announced that the $500 million health resources fund which is to be used to provide the facilities so that we can educate and train more doctors in Canada and which was to be expended in 15 years is to be stretched out over a longer period of time. The minister shakes his head but I am certain he made that announcement, and certainly that is what was understood by the provinces. I say that the provinces, which have the major responsibility for training doctors and for the provision of funds to expand the existing medical colleges and to build new ones such as the one that is being built, I understand, in the minister's own city of Hamilton, expected that the federal government would live up to its commitments. I suggest to the minister that the provinces, in making their plans to expand medical colleges, whether at the University of Toronto, in Manitoba or in British Columbia, and to build new medical colleges such as are being built at McMaster University in Hamilton or at the University of Sherbrooke, had a right to expect the federal government to live up
Government Organization to its commitments. I say that the government and the minister had no right to welsh on their commitments and to shortchange the provinces as they have done.
If I may, I would like to go back for a few minutes to the problem of medical research because we are facing a crisis which will affect not only medical research but the whole program of health services. I am sure I am less of an expert in these matters than the minister, but I have yet to meet anybody knowledgeable about the medical profession or about medical education who does not believe that without sufficient trained and qualified personnel at the medical colleges we cannot turn out enough doctors of the quality needed and who does not agree that we cannot get the necessary personnel for the medical colleges unless we are prepared to pay sufficient salaries to personnel with the ability to do the work which they want to do, namely, medical research. Yet in view of these shortages the government continues to ignore the specific, detailed and concrete recommendations made by every group which has looked at the problem of medical research and the problem of medical colleges in this country.
Let me take a few moments to summarize some of the things which are said in the most recent comprehensive survey that I have seen, namely, the 1966 Wood, Gundy survey. This is what they say:
-funds available from a variety of sources have been considerably short of those applied for. In 1965-66, almost $29 million of funds were requested by medical researchers for their work from agencies outside the universities (extra-mural agencies)- an amount representing minimum requests in view of the known shortage of funds. Only $21.5 million was made available.
This is what they say. In case the minister thinks my language was too strong, I will put the whole passage on the record as it appears at page 5 of the report:
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The effect on researchers can only be described as demoralising. Research effort is fragmented into small projects, the quality of research is impaired, uncertainty as to the ability to keep research teams together is general, and major new research programs are discouraged. There is a clear need to expand assistance to medical research in Canada if the present unfavourable climate is to be overcome and a longer-term expansion to be brought about.
The minister will, of course, tell me quite properly that we are spending substantially more on medical research in 1969 than in the
March 19, 1969

Government Organization year 1965-66 referred to in the report. But, Mr. Chairman, in that year we were meeting 70 per cent of requests for research funds while today we are meeting less than 70 per cent, according to the information I have. I therefore suggest that the fact that we are spending more money on research fails to deal with the crux of the problem which is that there is a tremendous shortfall in the effort made as seen by those who are most competent to judge.
The report goes into some detail. It says:
The capital needs of medical research in Canada for the period to the end of this decade amount to some $150 million. Since the announced size of the health resources fund is $500 million over a 15-year period, it would seem that the capital requirements for medical research-and it would appear, for health facilities as a whole-may not have been fully appreciated.
Today we are slowing down the rate at which we are paying out money from the health resources fund. The report goes on to say:
A doubling of the present level of research support in Canada would thus be needed to reach an appropriate level of research effort, and projection indicates that a further doubling to just over $100 million a year would be needed by the end of this decade.
Well, we are in the second to last year before the end of this decade and instead of the $100 million which the Wood, Gundy report recommends we are in fact giving to the Medical Research Council $31 million, roughly 30 per cent of what is called for. And, as I say, this report has been endorsed by all the prominent medical researchers and educationists.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this subject. I find nothing wrong with the proposal that the Medical Research Council should report to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In my view this is a sufficiently specialized field to justify the council reporting to the minister of health. I point out that the Food and Drug Directorate, which has a certain responsibility in connection with the pharmaceutical industry, is at present part of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and that in addition the department is responsible for making grants from the health resources fund for use by the medical teaching complexes which are vitally concerned with medical

research. The department is also concerned with the allocation of funds to hospitals, and a certain amount of research is carried out on the basis of these grants. For these reasons I believe it is on the whole in the best interests of medical research in this country that the council should report to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
When the affairs of the Medical Research Council were examined before Christmas it was found that a considerable proportion of its research funds was allocated to studies carried out in conjunction with the universities. The allocation of research projects was done by members of the medical colleges acting as members of the Medical Research Council. I should like to draw attention to certain anomalies and shortcomings which have arisen in connection with the health resources fund and the allocation of money from that fund.
Three years ago the government of the day promised $500 million over a period of years for the building of medical research complexes. This announcement was greeted with enthusiasm by the medical and teaching professions and a great effort was made by all the medical colleges to plan these complexes with a 15-year program in mind. Mr. Chairman, planning takes a minimum of five years to carry out, plus another five, tentatively. And at the end of that time a further period of five years may even be required. So it may take 15 years to plan a medical complex and bring it to fruition. Obviously, if there is any hitch in the program the effect can be doubly detrimental.
Last November the government in an atmosphere of stringency decided that the period preceding reassessment of this project should be shortened and today it looks as though the program of grants to these medical complexes may be reviewed in two years time, at which point funds may be either increased or restricted. I urge the minister to try to project farther into the future in determining what these treatment and teaching complexes are to receive. At the present time there is a great deal of uncertainty as to what may be in store for everyone concerned at the end of two years.
So far as the medical colleges are concerned, I am told on high authority from a teacher in one of the universities that they are spending approximately 10 per cent on research though it is considered desirable to spend upwards of 30 per cent of available funds on this work. When funds for research
March 19, 1969

are not available, medical colleges lose good men who tend to go to the United States where conditions are better and the tenure is longer. I therefore urge the minister to give those responsible for the teaching complexes an assurance as to what they may expect over the long term. If funds are not likely to be available, they will make plans accordingly.
We are about to embark on a medicare scheme which will require the services of many doctors and paramedical personnel. It seems to me that however we cut back in connection with medical care and activities, the research end should not suffer. In the long run, good research will bring about a reduction of the number of people involved in the actual care of patients or at least, for the level of care we shall need, fewer people will be required. I feel that the change now proposed in the system of reporting to the ministry is a sound one.

Mr. Chairman, medical research is a subject that has come to the fore today along with, I hope, the Science Council of Canada. Both matters are of extreme importance to Canada.
I am given to understand that because of conditions in Canada, particularly in our medical schools where inadequate funds for research are provided, many of our specialists and graduates with high standing are leaving Canada and going to other countries, particularly the United States, where they can undertake research. In addition, if research funds are not made available we may see more of our medical men leaving Canada to undertake research elsewhere. This has a great effect on the fundamental training of doctors in our universities. I am told that our best medical teachers in the universities want to do research work as well as teaching. In other words, they are not willing to vegetate in their chosen branch of the profession while training new doctors. In addition to teaching facilities they must have available research facilities which I am told are sadly lacking in Canada.
Some hon. members have already said that the budget for medical research this year has been increased by 10 per cent. It is estimated that it ought to be increased by 30 per cent if we are to keep pace with the tremendous growth in medical knowledge. That much money has not been promised and many
Government Organization medical researchers and specialists are worried because they may not be able to undertake research here and will have to leave Canada if they are to do so.
Bearing these factors in mind, may I draw Your Honour's attention to clause 56(2)(a) which says that the council is authorized to:
-expend, for the purposes of this Part, any money appropriated by Parliament for the work of Council or received by the Council through the conduct of its operations;
Clearly, therefore, under this clause there is provision for the expenditure of money on medical research. The best way of helping our medical schools is by spending money on research facilities for teachers. I therefore ask the minister, what funds will be devoted to medical research under clause 56 and how and when these will be paid? It is necessary for the minister, since we are considering a new set-up for the Medical Research Council, to assure the medical profession and its teachers and researchers that the federal government, through the Medical Research Council or otherwise, will provide funds to allow teachers to undertake research within the medical schools. If the minister can give that kind of assurance, not only will he have reassured the members of the medical profession but he will have boosted the esteem in which the Medical Research Council will be held.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the government, after nearly a year in office, has presented no clear statement of objectives and priorities for the nation. As a result public policy in all areas is haphazard and ad hoc. In short, it is completely inadequate. Nowhere is this process more evident than in the general area of public policy for science and technology.
At present there is tremendous disillusionment, especially in the scientific community, concerning the lack of government direction and co-ordination for fresh and new approaches in the development of science and technology in Canada. This stems from the following unpalatable facts. First of all, there was a series of cancellations in the scientific area, beginning with the cancellation of HARP, the McGill University high altitude research program. It was cancelled in 1966 without any adequate reasons being presented to the Canadian people. The aim of the project was related to an attempt to orbit satellites in space by using large cannon. The project received wide recognition for its simplicity as a scientific principle throughout the advanced world. Following its cancellation it was taken over by a number of American firms and financed by the United States government. At present it gives every indication of being a very successful scientific endeavour.
Second was the cancellation of the intense neutron generator program of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Given other priorities, including a greater emphasis on industrial applied research and development rather than basic research, this may have been the right decision. However, the point is that once again there are no publicly available reasons for justification of the decision. The only reason given for the cancellation of the ING program is that it is considered to be too expensive. When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announced cancellation of this program he referred to its relationship on the priority scale to the very many other demands on the national treasury. I ask, what scale of priorities? No one has told us. In fact there is no indication that the decision had any place in an over-all program of scientific priorities or that the money saved here would go toward some other project. Dr. W. G. Schneider, President of the National Research Council, has stated:

There may be sound reasons but, if so, the public has a right to know; I feel when decisions of this

kind are made, a rationale should be given. If they are handled in this way it tends to destroy morale. Everyone will always wonder what's going to get the chop next.
The third cancellation was in respect of The Queen Elizabeth Observatory. This project was scrapped even though millions of dollars had been spent on it. Once again the government has refused to release its report regarding the reasons for that decision.
A fourth point is that there is a significant lack of funds required for research into urban problems in Canada. As H. W. Hignett, President of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation told the Senate special committee studying science policy; C.M.H.C. has a mere $10 million revolving fund for assistance in this area. Everyone who is involved in research knows that this is a mere pittance. Government programs for industrial-scientific research and development are completely inadequate.
Last week about this time I devoted a whole speech to this subject so I shall not go over the same ground again except to say it is a fact worth repeating that the federal government is spending over 50 per cent of the money devoted to research and development in the military sector. This is something about which we as Canadians should be deeply concerned. These things, plus additional factors such as the tremendous expansion in government oceanographic research announced in January and the successful satellite research program which is being conducted by the new Department of Communications, clearly reveal that we do not have a coherent, cogent, highly motivated technological and research program in this country.
Senator Lamontagne, hardly an enemy of the government and chairman of the Senate committee, stated that scientists running federal research projects have so little supervision by parliament that they constitute an almost autonomous republic of science. He went on to state that government sponsored scientific research has never been reviewed systematically and said that even cabinet to his knowledge paid very little attention to it except when it was appraising on rare occasions specific and major programs. Senator Lamontagne has discovered in his committee's investigation that there are at least 100 boards and committees comprising about 700 scientists dealing with government research and development. He said that for all practical purposes the supervision and direction of those activities are left to scientists acting in

an administrative or advisory capacity. Decisions of social merit and human welfare cannot be left exclusively to scientists no matter how well motivated they may be as individuals.
After this very brief rundown of some unpalatable facts in respect of scientific development I should like to turn to the government's reorganization proposal. As the Glas-sco commission pointed out as long ago as 1958, there are basic contradictions and conflicts in the institutional environment regarding the determination of science policy in the government. The National Research Council should not be looked upon as the adviser to the government on scientific priorities since it is competing for the very same funds allocated in this area.
The Privy Council committee on scientific and industrial research, whose purpose it was to determine priorities, has been completely inactive since it was first established in 1916. It has been estimated that it has met only a dozen times since 1916. The establishment of the Science Council and Science Secretariat in
1965	and 1966 to fill this role has clearly shown severe limitations. The secretariat was to serve two masters, the Privy Council office with advice on scientific matters to the Prime Minister and also the Science Council of Canada as its secretary. This conflict of interest was obvious to all except the government.
The new legislation in the bill before the house merely gives the Science Council the same status and independence as the Economic Council of Canada. In other words, it will now hire its own staff rather than share with the government the staff of the science Secretariat. Thus the council's report will no longer be examined by those who participate in its implementation. The purpose of the Science Council when it was established in
1966	was to offer advice on public policy with regard to science and technology and to examine the role of our scientific effort in relation to Canada's aspirations. However, the Science Council has found itself confronted with the same difficulties in the formulation of objectives as were experienced by the Economic Council of Canada. Goals were established without any view of the relative importance of each and thus, for example, space and water resources programs were given priority by the Science Council in its last annual report merely for the bad reason that detailed proposals for implementation of these programs existed at the time.

As Professor Lithwick of Carleton University pointed out in recent correspondence in Science Forum of April 1968, the evaluation of a particular scientific project must be compared on the basis of whether the results of this form of public investment lare more valuable than the returns from an equivalent amount of funds invested elsewhere and not only in scientific research and development. I agree with Professor Lithwick that it is futile to argue as justification for particular projects that we have sufficient scientific manpower or that additional scientists and engineers will be employed, especially when he says that the housing industry is falling short of our minimum needs and our atmosphere and waterways are becoming dangerously polluted. In other words, a very serious consideration of the whole range of social and scientific priorities must be gone into. However, this is not the fault of the Science Council; it is the fault of the government in not assigning priorities in accordance with Canadian needs and aspirations and thereby giving no direction to the great potential role of science and technology in our country to meet these needs.
In recent months the government has considered setting up a ministry of science responsible for co-ordinating scientific research and development programs. At a press conference on August 14 the Prime Minister said that a science ministry was one possible mechanism for co-ordinating and checking on government research and development projects. I see the President of the Treasury Board smiling. He is well aware that the Prime Minister has changed his mind.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Following that one observation the Prime Minister stated he had some doubts about the desirability of asking the President of the Treasury Board to retain cabinet responsibility for science as chairman of the Privy Council committee on scientific and industrial research. The Prime Minister said that although the President of the Treasury Board knows a great deal about scientific research and was keenly interested, "as President of the Treasury Board he may have divided interests in the amount of money we would want to invest in that and perhaps I would not want to put him in a position of having to argue against himself". I agree.
However, the President of the Treasury Board in two recent speeches has completely ruled out any meaningful institutional changes in research and science policy. He

has acknowledged that better co-ordination and direction of scientific effort is needed but feels that modifications in the existing machinery will correct the situation. These modifications include the change in the status of the Science Council and more activities by the Privy Council committee on scientific and industrial research. The conflict that the Prime Minister discussed in August apparently is no longer an important factor.
One thing is clear: either the government does not know what it is doing in science or it is indifferent to Canada's scientific needs. Immediate action is required on the question of decision-making processes in scientific and technological matters. Three years have passed since the Science Council was set up; five years have gone by since the Science Secretariat was established. The debate on science policy has been going on for nearly a decade with scientists and technologists becoming impatient for results. I think the President of the Treasury Board has encountered a little of this feeling, perhaps particularly during his recent speech in Toronto where he suffered some disillusionment.
The New Democratic Party in 1967 adopted a resolution that the present functions of the Science Council and the Science Secretariat be taken over by the establishment of a department of science and technology with its own cabinet minister. The new minister and his department would be responsible for science policy, ensuring that activities of other departments involved in science would fit into one national policy. This department's responsibility would basically be in respect of a broad point of view, organizing, co-ordinating and controlling all federal science activities, but the minister would have no other departmental operating responsibilities.
This proposal was made some two years ago. It seemed to me to be good then and it seems to me to be good now. This is something the government should have taken up. I should like to hear the President of the Treasury Board, when he gets on his feet in a few minutes, give us his thoughts on the subject. I should like him to indicate why the government did not go ahead with this very reasonable proposal.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few comments on this subject. A lot can be said about the problems of science policy in Canada. A lot has been said in the past about the failure of the government to
March 19, 1969	COMMONS
develop a credible science policy. Much criticism has been directed at the government in respect of the cancellation of several scientific projects which had been started and whose cancellation was regrettable.
We should look forward and in doing so we must admit, first, that the present set-up for advising the cabinet on scientific matters has not worked out properly. I am not going to blame the President of the Treasury Board for this. I am sure he knows as well as anyone in the cabinet the intricacies of the science and research facilities within the government services. He knows very well, as do all of us, that research facilities are divided among the National Research Council, the Defence Research Board and the Science Council, formerly the Science Secretariat of the Privy Council. These services are also being performed by various other government agencies. I would not suggest that all these branches in various departments should be gathered up and pulled together into a new department. This would merely complicate an issue which at the present time is complicated enough.
In respect of pollution control the same situation applies. Many departments of the federal and provincial governments are involved. It would not be good policy to withdraw these activities from each of these departments and put them into one department. However, I do suggest that the scientific community, as far as I can gather, has the dreadful feeling that it is not getting through to the government. These people feel they do not have a minister or a spokesman with no other duty than to advise the cabinet on matters of science, research and technology, someone who would attempt to co-ordinate the efforts of these various groups. I know there is a real feeling of frustration in the scientific community. This was evidenced when these various projects were cancelled. In point of fact the scientific community does not have the feeling that an on-going science policy is being developed.
We are now dealing with the Science Council of Canada which is doing good work at the present time. The council has a number of very eminent members. If its chairman were within the cabinet structure it would be much more effective. I think the general feeling in the scientific community is that there is no voice in the cabinet to speak for it.
It has been said before that there is some conflict of interest. In other words, the President of the Treasury Board in reporting on
DEBATES	6839
Government Organization scientific matters does have a problem in that he cannot argue with himself too much in certain areas because he might win and someone else would lose. To that extent there is a difficult situation. This problem is very much in the minds of various people in the research and scientific community.
The President of the Treasury Board has other very heavy duties. He is not directly responsible for many of the research establishments I have mentioned. They come under the jurisdiction of other ministers who have equal status in the cabinet. Therefore there is in the set-up a lack of direct communication with the cabinet by the scientific community in respect of the development of scientific policy.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The Science Council has published some very good papers. On the subjects they have selected they have carried out a great deal of research and the papers have been well prepared. But there is also the feeling that they are not quite dealing with priorities and are just doing patchwork. In the United States the president has an adviser on science. We in Canada do not have this type of organization, and an adviser to the Prime Minister would not be within the cabinet. An adviser to the cabinet would have to be within it if the scientific community is to feel it is being fairly treated.
I have set out the problems as I see them. I think there must be an answer. There ought to be within the cabinet structure a minister who has no responsibilities other than to report on science and act as scientific adviser. I believe that such a minister does not need a department of government; he needs a small and competent research staff of senior scientists who can advise him.
So far as the bill before us is concerned, the move to upgrade the Science Council and make it a corporation with a structure of its own is a good thing. We certainly would support the principle. However, I ask the minister whether he can straighten out some statements he made recently, or at least was reported to have made, that there was no need for co-ordination of on-going research programs in Canada. The minister said that a minister of science and technology was not required.
Unfortunately we hear these reports second-hand. We get them out of newspapers in many cases. Sometimes the minister provides us with the text of a speech he intends

If the minister can give us the assurance that the government is seriously considering this question and the lack of a person within the cabinet who has no responsibilities other than to advise on science and technology, he will do a great deal to relieve the fears of many people in the scientific community.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been most interested to listen to the comments of the two members who have just spoken, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. In relation to the amendments proposed in the bill relating to the Science Council and Science Secretariat, I am glad they both expressed approval of them. Therefore securing passage should present no difficulty.
I should like to deal with some observations made in relation to government science policy generally and the kind of institutions, the kind of structure, that might best operate to give the most effective, the most adequate response to scientific needs. I think one thing should be made clear. When the term ''science" is used, and it has been used by these two gentlemen

this is particularly so in its use in the bill-it relates to the natural sciences and engineering, technology as it is called, rather than the social sciences or science as representing the accumulation of human knowledge for the betterment of mankind. When I use the term "science" it will be in relation to the natural sciences and technology.
One thing that perhaps should be borne in mind in relation to the current debate is the changing position of science, that is, the natural sciences and technology, and of scientists in North America today. There has been for some time now an inclination on the part of the North American public to regard science as likely to produce the answers to all our current problems and anything, therefore, done for, by or in the name of science is of itself good. There has arisen rather more recently a tendency, particularly in the United States and it is beginning to show in Canada, to question the value of research as such and to ask what are the results of research.

Merely to proclaim -that the purpose of the activity is research in itself unrelated to our current needs, our current functions, or indeed our longer-range objectives, is not as accurate as it was a few years ago.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
According to the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, the scientists feel that they are not getting through to the government. I suppose this is a manifestation of a lack of support in respect of these questions that are being asked as to the value and relevance of some research that is being done and in particular of the unwillingness of the government and of the public to support all scientific research, regardless of its class, kind, relevance or quality, merely because it is research. This questioning is understandable. I myself think it is a good thing and am very much encouraged by the growing public interest that is being shown in science and technology, not only by scientists themselves who have always had it but by a large spectrum of both the industrial and academic public.
What are our needs? These needs, put into a time framework in terms of science and technology, are both long range and short range, or immediate. The analysis of scientific objectives over the long range and the determination of long range priorities in respect of which we would not expect immediate results is not an easy task for the operating element of the government to undertake. Governments by their very nature are preoccupied, unless they are underworked, with dealing with day to day problems that are certainly not much longer than medium range, and there never seems to be adequate time for reflection and consideration of the longer range perspectives and objectives and the contemplative consideration of how best they can be met and how they fit into a total framework. This, then, was one of the reasons for establishing the Science Council of Canada which was, rather like the Economic Council of Canada, to do in the scientific and technological field what the Economic Council was to do in the economic field for the country, namely, to propound longer-range objectives and the priorities which should be attached to these and to suggest a long-term means of meeting them.
This is obviously a task which cannot be accomplished in a week. If it were as easy as that, the government would long ago have undertaken it itself within its own machinery.
March 19, 1969

But it is a difficult task that takes time and, more important, one should recognize that once this longer-range framework is established, immediate and specific achievement of it is unlikely. Since by definition it is long range, one cannot expect immediate results from the government or, indeed, immediate action on the part of the government or of the scientific community. If one accepts then that the function of the Science Council is to devise for Canada a framework over the long term into which our scientific endeavours, activities and policies should coherently fit, then I think we will have gone quite a long way to resolving some of the doubts that now exist.
As I have indicated, the perspective which principally engages the government's attention is very much shorter range than that which should be envisaged by the Science Council. I should add parenthetically that the objective in relation to the Science Council is not to have an organ which merely devises long-range policies for the federal government but to have a body which will enunciate long-range objectives in the science field for the whole of Canada, and this includes not only the federal government but provincial governments, the academic community, the industrial community, and anyone else who may be interested. So the Science Council would be expected to talk not merely to the federal government but to Canada, and it does this through the medium of its published reports of which the fourth, I remind hon. members, is modestly described as aiming toward a science policy. The Science Council does not pretend that in its short existence it has been able to formulate and enunciate all the long-range objectives, but it has made some progress in this direction, so that this in effect is a progress report.
So much then for the long-term framework. The federal government, in respect of scientific and technological research activities, is concerned) with a rather shorter period. Science, in the sense that I use the word, is a technique which is useful not in itself but as a means of accomplishing in an efficient and orderly way the human objectives that we all seek to reach. To this end everyone who is in charge of an operation of the government, no matter what his job or his station, should envisage the use of science and of scientific research in order to carry out his job more effectively. This means then that science cannot be separated from the day to day operations of the government departments or agencies; it must be an integral part of each and
Government Organization every one of them, and to the extent that the federal government is successful in integrating this scientific approach into the operations of government agencies it has been successful in its scientific policy.
As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka pointed out, it would be a denial of this principle to try to withdraw and segregate under one head all scientific research within the government. I heartily agree with the suggestion that these are now and must continue to be integral with the operations of all government departments. There are, however, some agencies which are devoted to scientific research as such, including applied research, and they have no other mission. We do not have many of these in the federal government, I am glad to say. Most of the research activities are an important appendage and a useful instrument in carrying out an objective or a mission of government agencies or departments. The large research effort of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources is not made for research itself but to make that department more effective and more able to carry out its basic mission.
But the National Research Council is an exception. Its function is to carry out fundamental research and applied research in a variety of fields which are perhaps not immediately and directly related to government departmental missions. By statute it reports to parliament through the minister appointed as chairman of the Privy Council committee on scientific and industrial research. So that a number of scientific research activities are carried out in the government, and the problem raised by both the hon. members who spoke is how these should be co-ordinated. One suggestion was that there should be a minister charged with such co-ordination who would have no other activity than this co-ordination. It was suggested that such a minister should be a senior minister, and I take it that that particular adjective is used' by the proponents of this scheme in the sense that it conveys a notion of a person with major influence as distinct from one heavy with years and honours but with little else.

Government Organization I hasten to add that I will not talk about the causeway. Indeed, since only 26 minutes are left before the supper adjournment I have too little time to put even the basic case before the committee, let alone develop any arguments to show how the matter of the causeway has been completely mishandled. It was all very well for the Prime Minister to backpeddle and say the causeway would not be built.
Very little has been said about transportation difficulties besetting the people of Prince Edward Island and still less about increases in ferry rates. There was a rumour two or three years ago when Mr. Pickersgill was in command that our ferry rates would be increased. The actual increase in respect of vehicles, was in the order of 50 per cent. We know that this is a period of inflation and rising costs. Nevertheless, the people of Prince Edward Island were justifiably upset when the increase of 50 per cent was introduced two years ago. Ferry rates were increased despite the assurance of the then minister of transport and the then government, represented by two ministers in the chamber this afternoon, that responsible authorities-presumably that was the Canadian Transport Commission-would hold a full series of hearings to determine the effect of the increase before the increase was introduced. That assurance was given on many occasions. Of course there were never any hearings and the rates were increased through the mechanism of doing away with the return ferry rate which had been in existence for many years. As a result the people of Prince Edward Island had to bear increased costs. We are told now that there is to be a further increase in rates of about 50 per cent. The total increase will then be 100 per cent of the old rates. And all this has taken place within the last two or three years.
We talk about responsible action to be taken by government departments. When one considers what has happened to Prince Edward Island ferry rates one must be shocked. I find it particularly shocking for the Minister of Transport not to have the decency to be present in the house this afternoon and discuss this matter. Considering the decision not to continue with construction of the causeway project, why has the minister agreed to these ferry rate increases? This is a particular affront to the people of Prince Edward Island. When we are all supposed to be concerned about maintaining good rela-t:ons between the provinces and the federal authority, this kind of cavalier handling of a
March 19. 1969

Government Organization basic question related to the economic and social future of this province is really contemptible.
There is little use in my elaborating on this question this afternoon, but I can tell you, Mr. Chairman, that the people of Prince Edward Island are profoundly disturbed that this government and the Minister of Transport should, after having cancelled the causeway project, go full speed ahead with an increase in ferry rates that will come into effect shortly for the Northumberland ferry service. The private company operating the other ferry service presumably was not consulted and no doubt it too will revise its rates upward. maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER STANDING ORDER S-O 26 NATIONAL DEFENCE FIRING OF A.B.M. WARHEADS OVER CANADIAN TERRITORY-MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, normally one would express regret at bringing members back on a Wednesday night, which is the only evening they have off all week. However, I have no apology to make for asking the house to debate a matter which I think is the most important problem of our age. Certainly, nothing is so important as the survival of the human race.
This is the first time in the history of mankind that man has had the power to commit social suicide. There have been countless wars throughout history. These wars have involved a few thousand, a few hundred thousand or even a few million people; and cities or even entire countries have been devastated. But for the first time in man's long evolution, he now has the power to destroy not only himself but all forms of life. Therefore, nothing can be more important than that we, as members of this house, should concern ourselves about any event which might lead to an escalation of nuclear arms and to a proliferation of nuclear missiles.
This matter came to a head last Friday, March 14, when President Nixon of the United States announced that his administration had decided to proceed with an A.B.M. system known as the Safeguard system. It should be recalled that the whole question of anti-ballistic missiles has been discussed for a long period of time. Many opinions have been expressed for and against in many parts of the world, including the United States. Some people in the United States Senate and the United States Congress have spoken out against the establishment of an A.B.M. system. Sometimes when one expresses some concern about this matter one is accused of being anti-American, unpatriotic or pro-Soviet Union. The fact of the matter is there are a
March 19, 1969

Firing of A.B.M. Warheads over Canada great many patriotic United States citizens who today are questioning very seriously, and criticizing very vigorously, the President's decision with regard to an A.B.M. System.
I notice that the New York Times, in an editorial of Monday, March 17 says this:
For all the surface persuasiveness of the President's assurances that he seeks to follow the course of moderation, the rationale on which he bases his decision provides fresh evidence that the arms race feeds on itself in a cycle that can never stop short of world annihilation.
The editor goes on to point out that while the President has based his decision on some 67 A.B.M.'s stationed around Moscow, the Pentagon has long recognized that these are already obsolete and that the planned American response involves more than 700 antimissile missiles and, through the use of MIRV multiple warheads, a probable fivefold increase in offensive delivery vehicles from 1,700 to more than 8,000.
So, many thoughtful people are raising honest questions about this whole matter. Let me very briefly, in my limited time, try to outline the story of the investigations and discussions that have gone on with regard to A.B.M.'s. The first proposal was for a complete A.B.M. system with Nike-X missiles. That was opposed by former defence secretary Robert McNamara. He appeared before the Senate Armed Services and Defence Appropriations Committee on January 26, 1967, and presented a 209 page brief. I shall not take the time of the house to quote from the brief extensively but I believe I could paraphrase his submission by saying that he objected to the proposal, first on the ground that it would not provide real security and that the United States would be spending large sums of money for something which in the end would provide it with little or no security. He argued that the United States security lay in its offensive capacity and its four to one ratio in respect of intercontinental ballistic missiles vis-a-vis the Soviet Union and its possession of the nuclear submarine armed with Polaris missiles.
His second objection before the Senate committee was that the construction of an extensive A.B.M. system could quite easily be the step that would trigger further escalation in the nuclear arms race. As hon. members know, Mr. McNamara, under pressure from the powerful military complex in the United States, finally agreed to what was known as this "thin line system" missile system. This was for use for defence against Mainland China only and not directed at the Soviet Union. Continued pressure from the chiefs of

staff and from the industries concerned resulted in the acquiescence and the announcement by President Johnson of what became known as the Sentinel system. This was to surround some of the major cities in the United States with A.B.M. bases. There was so much of an uproar in some of the cities in the United States that in the United States Congress that President Johnson decided to leave this matter in abeyance and dump it into the lap of the incoming president.
e (8:10 p.m.)
President Nixon has for some time been considering what his administration would do about the construction of the A.B.M. system. Last Friday he made an announcement that they were going to construct what he calls a Safeguard system which will not surround major centres of population but will be designed to protect the 11 Minuteman bases situated centrally throughout the United States.
In his statement the president was very careful to say that this decision on his part was not provocative and not meant to lead to nuclear escalation. I cannot do better than quote what was said in the Montreal Star on Monday, March 17 by James Eayrs, who is a well known author and acknowledged authority in respect of foreign affairs. In answering the president's statement that this' A.B.M. system would confer protection on the American people Mr. Eayrs said:
It Is likely to confer nothing of the sort. It offers protection only if the Soviet Union stands pat in the face of an addition to American power. Everything known about the dynamics of the arm's race, about the reflexes of its Russian contestants, suggests that the Soviet Union will not stand pat. Mr. Nixon's assurances that "the program is not provocative," that "the Soviet retaliation be retaliatory capability is not affected by our decision," are either naive or dishonest.
Someone may well ask, what business is it of Canada's what the United States does. I suggest that it is our business. It is our business because any action which could lead to a nuclear holocaust would have terrible consequences for the people of Canada. This was underlined this week by the Canadian chief disarmament negotiator in Geneva, Mr. George Ignatieff, who was formerly our representative at the United Nations, and is now stationed at Geneva. Mr. Ignatieff said:
-Canada is placed in the most dangerous position of any country by the galloping arm's race between the United States and the Soviet Union. If this race gets out of hand, it could be catastrophic for Canada which lies between the nuclear giants.

In respect of something which is of so great importance to Canada, it seems to me passing strange that the Canadian government should have had no intimation from the United States, and that there should have been no consultation. There can be no doubt about that. Hansard of March 17 at page 6684 records the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as having said in answer to the question I asked:
No, Mr. Speaker. We were notified of the decision, but there was no consultation in the sense that we might have been in a position to change the decision.
At page 6689 of Hansard for the same day, there is recorded a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) and the minister's answer. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked for similar information in these words:
-will the minister say when he . . . first received notification of the decision by the United States in this regard?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs replied:
Mr. Speaker, we were told of the decision immediately before it was announced.
I must say that many Canadians will feel as I do, that we who are neighbours and friends of the United States, with 4,000 or 5,000 miles of undefended border, have a right to better treatment than that. Canada is not a banana republic. We want to be friends and neighbours but not subservient.

Surely we have the right to be concerned about this decision by the United States in view of the fact Canadian territory is involved. As I said before, the missile bases are proposed to protect the Minuteman bases. Some of these will be close to the Canadian border. They will be protected by Spartani missiles with a range of not more than 400 miles. Certainly, all indications are that any interception will be planned over Canadian territory. I agree that the primary concern is not just where the anti-missiles will intercept these missiles. The primary concern is to prevent the escalation of nuclear armament and a nuclear war.
Surely, when the government deliberately designs an A.B.M. system for its own defence that is predicated on the interception of ballistic missiles over a neighbour's territory, the very least it could do is consult with the neighbour prior to making the decision.

speechtext:
I thank the house for its indulgence, Mr. Speaker, and I shall take only a few more minutes. I am sure that members in all parts of the house, and Canadians generally, will be pleased that the right hon. Prime Minister is going to Washington next week. I hope the Prime Minister will tell the President of the United States that we in this house, and the people of this country, are concerned about the decision he has taken, a decision which Mr. James Eayrs in the article to which I referred earlier called "black Friday".
I hope he will tell the President of the United States that we feel justified in being concerned because of our geographical position and our long association with the United States. As neighbours and friends of the United States we feel we might have been given an opportunity to express our opinion. I hope the Prime Minister will tell the President of the United States that we believe there is a serious danger that this action, without providing any amount of security for the American people or ourselves, could trigger a very serious nuclear arms race.
I am sure the Prime Minister realizes that this is one of the most important missions he has ever undertaken. I am sure he realizes that he will go to Washington with the hopes and aspirations of the Canadian people on his shoulders, with the hopes of all humanity who yearn for peace. We hope he will succeed in getting reconsideration of this matter, and that there will be agreement for consultation in' the future before action is taken which could affect Canada's safety and welfare.
If the Prime Minister is able to accomplish that, I tell him he will have the gratitude and indebtedness of people in all parts of this country. However, if he does not speak out for Canada and take an independent stand, which I think he is capable of doing, this is a matter which will be on his conscience for a long time.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose that seldom does it happen that the leader of a government can say he welcomes debate under this standing order. In this particular case however I say very sincerely that I do welcome debate. This is a most urgent and difficult matter, and before I go to see the President of the United States I am anxious to hear the views of the leaders of the opposition parties on this important subject. I say this because I realize
DEBATES	6851
Firing of A.B.M. Warheads over Canada that we are discussing here one aspect of a problem which involves the fate of all mankind. I know it is necessary that we, as the government of Canada must speak about the protection of Canadians, about the protection of our cities, and about the protection we believe our nation deserves. I know, too, that as the government, we must also ensure that the international laws which apply to our air space are respected.
Nevertheless when I answered questions in the house on this subject the other day I said very frankly that in a real sense these were secondary concerns of ours, and I will explain why this is so. We believe that this whole matter is not one in which only Canadians are involved. I echo what the leader of the New Democratic Party said when I say that we believe that this whole matter is one which involves the fate of humanity. It is for this reason that we on this side of the house take the position that before sitting down to bargain with the United States on where the system should be located, on whether they have considered where the fallout would occur, whether or not it would be on Canadian cities, we want to remain free to say that we condemn this system entirely. We want to be free to disapprove of it, which we would not be if we said to them: "Please set it down here or there and please make sure that you do not destroy us in the process of protecting yourselves".
This is the reason that I, and the government take this stand. When I do speak to the President I will not be in the position of asking for a little more protection for Canadians but rather will be able to put questions to him about whether his decision constitutes an escalation and an increase of the danger of nuclear warfare or whether it is merely an operation which adds to the stability of the deterrent system.
Some years ago Canadians did not have such a difficult decision to make. Other countries in history have lived for years in the fear of destruction, although perhaps not nuclear destruction. Wars in other lands very often constituted an imminent danger of destruction to many nations. For us in Canada however, it is the first time that we have been faced with such a problem. It is only four and a half decades ago that Senator Dan-durand was able to say to the League of Nations that we in Canada "live in a fireproof house, far from inflammatory materials".
This is no longer the case. Our house is not fireproof and, as we know, inflammatory
March 19, 1969
6852	COMMONS
Firing of A.B.M. Warheads over Canada materials are no longer very far from it. Science has made us all neighbours in this world. The progress of science and technology is such that one nation cannot hope to save itself alone. Talented writers have used various expressions to express this result. Mr. McLuhan speaks about the "global village", and he is right; we are truly living in a global village. Barbara Ward talks about a "Spaceship Earth". I suggest these expressions convey, in a true sense, the feeling of solidarity that we as Canadians have with all nations on this earth.

Consequently, the Canadian government is as concerned about this subject as the members of the opposition and all Canadians.
I repeat that we wish to ensure the security of Canadians and especially that decisions that might affect the future of humanity are not taken without our participation.
I think the debate taking place this evening is intended to determine a policy which will ensure the security of humanity, including that of Canadians.

How we manifest our concern for humanity, so as to make our desire for survival into an effective policy, is the subject of this debate tonight. There are a few general principles which guide this government in establishing such a policy. The first refers to the stability of the deterrent system. This system exists as a deterrent because of the knowledge on both sides that the other has a destructive power capable of annihilating it. It is the credibility of the system which ensures its stability. This is a fragile and dangerous balance. If the system is to retain its credibility, we must seek to make sure that it does not lose its balance; we must make sure that there is no escalation of nuclear armament systems, no rushing ahead by one of the two centres of military power on this earth, the TJ.S.S.R. and the U.S.A., so that the other is in fear of being destroyed without having the capacity to destroy its opponent. It is this very delicate balance that must be maintained until we are able through other means to ensure arms limitation and arms reduction agreements which are truly workable and effective.
The second principle is that Canada should continue to participate in the Geneva negotiations, as it has through one of its most able ambassadors, Mr. George Ignatieff, who has


been speaking for Canada in these matters. We must continue to do so because we believe that deterrence is a very delicate, sensitive and dangerous system, and we must work with all our energy to seek out other avenues to arms limitations and reductions.
Another principle that we must apply is to attempt to prevent the further proliferation or indeed escalation of nuclear armament systems. To each of the countries concerned, such an escalation is an extremely costly business and can only entail an extremely costly retaliation of the defensive system of the other country. This is doubly serious because it places these great great nations of the world in a less favourable position to meet the other challenges facing humanity, the challenges of domestic poverty and of slowly developing nations, for example. We, therefore, believe this escalation to be a dangerous thing for this additional reason that it prevents countries from solving these other problems. Then again, it is dangerous in itself because the more sensitive these systems get the more complex they become and the greater the danger of accident. Already, we are beginning to wonder whether these systems are not so complicated and intricate that the decision to start a nuclear holocaust will be made by a computer or by some officials who really have not the time in which to weigh all the imponderable elements before reaching a decision.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
These are the principles which govern us. But because this government is not yet in possession of sufficient information to make the necessary judgment as to the decision taken last Friday by the President of the United States, we are keeping an open mind on this. The leader of the New Democratic Party says we have evidence of escalation, and he has quoted some evidence. But I think it would be counter-productive in connection with any talks I might have with the President if, before going to Washington, this government took the position that there was escalation; that the United States was guilty; that we were not giving them a chance to explain their point of view, and that we condemn them out of band.
This is the reason the government is not taking an attitude of condemnation. It is one of interrogation, one of seeking information; it is one of finding out reasons for this action by the United States and then making up our minds.

speechtext:
If, Mr. Speaker, after receiving all the information, we are led to the view that the A.B.M. system constitutes escalation and is conducive to greater peril for mankind, then we shall condemn it. We shall tell the United States that we disapprove. If, on the other hand, we are convinced that the A.B.M. system is necessary though regrettable as a move by the United States, then we shall have to decide whether or not we shall participate in the operation of that system. Let me remind this house that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux), and myself have made clear on several occasions that the space defence system, the A.B.M. system now contemplated, has not been integrated into NORAD but is something outside NORAD. It follows in all fairness that we cannot, while refusing to participate in this A.B.M. system, while taking the position that it must remain outside NORAD, complain that the United States is not consulting with us.
The leader of the N.D.P., who answered a few questions by the Secretary of State for External Affairs must, I think, sense this contradiction. On the one hand, he complains that the Americans have not consulted us, as they should, while on the other hand, his party has on various occasions taken the position that we should withdraw from NATO. I was happy to hear the leader of the N.D.P. clarify his position on this issue. He said in answer to the minister that we were allies in NORAD and NATO, and he supported the idea that we should be friends and allies of the United States. Well, the New Democratic party has obviously reached the conclusion of its external affairs review. We have not reached that position yet, and we still reserve our judgment. We may decide to stay in NATO or we may decide to pull out. We may decide to stay in NORAD or we may decide to pull out. But we shall have to be consistent with ourselves, and if we stay in NORAD we shall have to ask ourselves whether we want it to include some degree of control over, the A.B.M. system, or not. If our answer is we do not, we shall not be in possession of a very strong negotiating point with the United States.
We might, of course, protest that they should not be using our air space or that they should not contemplate exploding anti-ballistic missiles over Canadian soil. However, I repeat, as I said the other day in the house, 2S180-4341
Firing of A.B.M. Warheads over Canada that this would be a fairly academic consideration, Mr. Speaker, because should the system begin to fire it will mean our efforts to preserve the peace and the safety of the world have failed, and I think the question of national air space would be secondary. I do not mean to say-and I believe I am answering the question which was put to me-that we are not informed. The minister said this afternoon, and I repeat it, that we have been informed to an impressive degree about what the United States is doing. I believe the Minister of National Defence will reveal later in this debate that we have a lot of information on the technological work being done there in the field of deterrents. However, we do not have all the information and, in particular, we do not have a veto over the operation of the system. If this house feels we should participate in decisions concerning this system it may be we shall have to become partners in the A.B.M. system. But this is a decision we are not yet prepared to make.
We want, first, to be convinced that the system is necessary. If it is not necessary we shall condemn it. If not, we shall seek the kind of protection which the opposition suggested we obtain for Canadian cities. I do not believe I should carry on this debate further. Essentially, I am saying we do not yet have sufficient information on the basis of which to reach a decision on the position taken by the United States last Friday. We do not wish, before going to Washington, to judge that position out of hand. Therefore, I believe I shall welcome this occasion as an opportunity to hear what other members of this house have to say. Before any final conclusion is reached, we shall always consider that it is our duty to look for methods of settling disputes through negotiation rather than through any form of escalation of deterrent systems.
Let me, before ending, read to the house a fitting quotation from Madam Barbara Ward, words which are deservedly well known. I quote:
In the last few decades mankind has been overcome by the most fateful change in its entire history. Modern science and technology have created so close a network of communication, transport, economic interdependence-and potential nuclear destruction-that planet earth, on its journey through infinity, has acquired the fellowship and the vulnerability of a spaceship.
In such a close community, there must be rules for survival.
It is in search of those rules for survival, Mr. Speaker, that I shall be speaking to the President of the United States next week.
